J1.evidence: Arabic «أكد في كتابه «الإتقان» صحة الحديث بشهادة واحد وعشرين صحابيا ذكروه»: ذكروه is a plural verb whose subject is the twenty-one Companions and whose object هـ is the hadith, i.e. 'twenty-one Companions who mentioned/narrated it'. EN renders 'twenty-one Companions whom he named', making al-Suyuti the subject and the Companions the object — wrong meaning (singular agent, reversed roles). TR 'onu zikreden' is correct.

J2.evidence: Arabic «أكد في كتابه «الإتقان» صحة الحديث بشهادة واحد وعشرين صحابيا ذكروه»: ذكروه is a plural verb whose agent is the 21 Companions and whose object is the ḥadīth ('who mentioned/narrated it'). EN 'twenty-one Companions whom he named' makes al-Suyuti the agent and the Companions the object - wrong meaning (TR 'onu zikreden' is correct). Fix: 'twenty-one Companions who mentioned it'.

J1.evidence: Arabic «ولبسوا السيجان وهي الطيالسة المدورة الواسعة» is rendered 'They wore al-saylasān' — a different word (طيلسان-like), the source word is السيجان (al-sījān); and «وسورة الخمر وسوارها حدتها» is rendered 'sawrat al-khamr and its sūrāt' — the source has سوارها (suwāruhā), not sūrāt. Both mis-render the lexical headwords of the source. In addition the EN vocabulary section gives the Arabic headwords only in Latin transliteration (e.g. «سوّج وسيّج الكرم» -> 'Sawwaja and sayyaja l-karma') where TR keeps them in Arabic script, against the rule that discussed words stay in Arabic script.

J2.evidence: Arabic «ولبسوا السيجان وهي الطيالسة المدورة الواسعة» -> EN 'They wore al-saylasān' names a different word (the headword is السيجان, al-sījān, plural of sāj; الطيالسة is the gloss). Arabic «وسورة الخمر وسوارها حدتها» -> EN 'sawrat al-khamr and its sūrāt' misrenders سوارها (suwāruhā). Both are wrong renderings of the lexical headwords; fix: keep السيجان and سوارها in Arabic script.

J1.evidence: On the flagged point: Abu Hayyan's «عارية من رابط يربطها بالمبتدأ وليست نفس المبتدأ في المعنى فلا تحتاج إلى رابط» literally = 'and it is not the mubtada itself in meaning so as not to need a link'; EN 'and it is not the same as the mubtadaʾ in meaning, so it does need a link' flips the wording of the negated fa-clause; the logical upshot (a link is required) is the same, so this alone is a paraphrase rather than a wrong meaning, though a literal rendering is preferable. However EN has an unmarked addition elsewhere: Mutanabbi's «ولو قلم ألقيت في شقّ رأسه ... من السقم ما غيرت من خط كاتب» is rendered 'from illness [emaciation]' — '[emaciation]' is not in the Arabic and is not a Translator's note. Needs fix (move into a note, and preferably render the Abu Hayyan clause literally).

J2.evidence: Abu Hayyan quote «عارية من رابط يعود على المثل وليست نفس المبتدأ في المعنى فلا تحتاج إلى رابط»: the Arabic has the negation فلا تحتاج ('[such that] it would not need a link', i.e. it is not the mubtada itself so as to dispense with a link). EN 'and it is not the same as the mubtadaʾ in meaning, so it does need a link' drops the negation لا, translating a different text (silent rewording). Fix: render the negation as written ('so that it would not need a link'), with a Translator's note if needed.
